title: Knowledge Base Authoring
scenario: Mr. Thompson has noticed that the same Wi-Fi authentication problem has generated 14 tickets over the past month. He asks you to author a knowledge base article so that any technician — and faculty power users — can resolve the common case without opening a ticket. The article should target the right audience and not leak sensitive information.
impact: Operational: a well-written KB article reduces repeat ticket volume, improves first-time resolution, and shortens training time for new technicians. A poorly written article creates confusion and support burden.
objectives: Identify the recurring pattern from the past 30 days of tickets
Define the target audience: technician or end user
Draft the KB article using the school standard template
Include symptoms, scope check, and step-by-step resolution
Add troubleshooting decision points and a clear escalation path
Review the article for accuracy, tone, and security before publishing

evidence.description: Ticket pattern report showing the recurring Wi-Fi issue frequency and common cause
Draft KB article in the school template with all required sections
Completed peer review checklist confirming accuracy, tone, and security

decisionPoints.prompt: Who is the primary audience for this KB article?

options.label: End users (faculty and staff) — they can self-serve the most common case
options.feedback: Correct — if the issue is recurring and the fix is simple, an end-user-targeted article deflects the most tickets. Pair it with a technician companion article for edge cases.

options.label: Technicians only — keep it as an internal playbook for the help desk
options.feedback: A technician-only article is acceptable but reduces the deflection impact. Aim for end-user first when the fix is safe and self-serviceable.

options.label: Write one article that tries to serve both audiences at the same time
options.feedback: One article for two audiences is rarely effective — the language and depth are different. Write two articles, or two sections with a clear handoff.

decisionPoints.prompt: The draft article includes the step 'unlock the account in the directory using the admin tool.' What is the right editorial decision?

options.label: Keep it as written — technicians need the unlock step and end users can be told to call the desk
options.feedback: The unlock step is sensitive. It belongs in a technician-only article, not in an end-user-facing article. Split the article.

options.label: Remove the unlock step from the end-user article and replace with 'call the service desk' or 'open a ticket'
options.feedback: Correct — remove the sensitive step from the end-user article. Provide a clear self-service path that does not require admin credentials or actions.

options.label: Add a warning label and keep the unlock step visible to all readers
options.feedback: A warning label is not enough. Sensitive steps should not be exposed to end users at all — that is a documentation and security problem.

ticket.initialDescription: Mr. Thompson requests a KB article for the recurring Wi-Fi authentication issue. 14 tickets in 30 days. Target: reduce repeat volume, support both technicians and end users where appropriate.

state.common_root_cause: account lockout after 5 failed password attempts

nodes.title: Analyze the ticket pattern
nodes.body: Pull the past 30 days of Wi-Fi authentication tickets. Note the common root cause, the affected users, the affected locations, and the first-time resolution rate. Confirm the recurring pattern is real and worth an article.

nodes.title: Choose the audience
nodes.body: Decide who the article is primarily for: end users, technicians, or split into two.

nodes.title: Draft the KB article
nodes.body: Use the school KB template. Fill in: title, audience, summary, symptoms, scope, step-by-step resolution, escalation path, and related articles. Save the draft as evidence.

nodes.title: Review for sensitive content
nodes.body: The draft includes the step 'unlock the account in the directory using the admin tool.' Decide how to handle it.

nodes.title: Peer review
nodes.body: Have a peer review the article against the checklist: accuracy, tone, security, screenshots, escalation path. Save the completed checklist as evidence.

nodes.title: Publish and announce
nodes.body: Publish the article in the KB platform with the right audience tag. Send a brief announcement to the help desk and reference it from the new-ticket template.
nodes.prompt: Write the announcement to the help desk team explaining the new KB article, when to use it, and how to link to it from a ticket.

nodes.title: Debrief
nodes.body: Review the KB authoring workflow. Key lessons: write for the right audience, never expose sensitive steps to end users, and always peer review before publishing.

kbOpportunity: KB authoring checklist: confirm recurring pattern → define audience → use school template → review for sensitive content → peer review → publish with audience tag → measure deflection.
